overview: This card covers the ancient city and state centred on Monte Albán, not every Zapotec community. Archaeology places its founding around 500 BCE, before the atlas begins in 323 BCE. One coarse 12-vertex regional polygon repeats through 800 CE; it is neither a surveyed city boundary nor a proven state frontier. Dates, population and political reach remain archaeological estimates.

periods.title: Mountaintop foundation and early growth
periods.summary: People founded a new capital high above the Oaxaca Valley; its population and defensive works grew rapidly.

periods.title: Urban expansion and early state power
periods.summary: The plaza, terraces, writing and regional administration expanded alongside conflict, tribute and satellite communities.

periods.title: Classic-period height and distant connections
periods.summary: Monumental building, elaborate tombs, trade and contact with Teotihuacan marked a powerful regional capital.

periods.title: Late Classic city and shifting centres
periods.summary: Monte Albán remained important while political activity also developed at nearby centres such as Atzompa.

periods.title: Depopulation and loss of capital status
periods.summary: The polity fragmented and much of the city emptied; the place remained sacred and continued to receive visitors and offerings.

sections.title: A mountain remade into a capital

items.text: Monte Albán was founded around 500 BCE on a ridge about 400 metres above the valley. Early builders cleared and levelled space, raised defensive works and attracted thousands of residents. University of Michigan researchers model it as one of Mexico’s earliest states, formed amid rivalry and conquest. That is an archaeological reconstruction, not a surviving royal chronicle.

The Main Plaza stretched roughly 300 metres, while builders cut terraces, dams, channels, pyramids and artificial mounds into the mountain. This was a huge achievement in planning and organized labour. It also displays inequality and state power: ordinary workers moved stone, soil, food and water so rulers could turn a difficult summit into a political and sacred landscape.

Carved captive figures, defensive walls and burned rival centres show that state building was not only clever architecture. Monumental images presented defeated or sacrificed people and helped rulers advertise force. The familiar nickname “Danzantes” can sound cheerful, but many scholars read the figures as dead, injured or captive bodies. A field trip should not turn violence into a dance party.

Monte Albán exchanged people, objects and styles with Teotihuacan, about 500 kilometres away; archaeologists found a Zapotec neighbourhood there and Teotihuacan-style material in Oaxaca. Sources disagree about whether later relations were peaceful or involved conquest. The safest discovery is connection, not a tidy friendship-or-invasion answer where the evidence still invites debate.

sections.title: Writing, rulers, exchange and skilled work

items.text: Zapotec writing at Monte Albán recorded calendar names, dates, leaders, actions and places on stone. A keyboard-friendly sample is “13 Owl,” the conventional reading of the name beside a seated ruler on Stela 1. The original is a number-and-picture glyph, not those English letters. Longer inscriptions remain partly undeciphered, so nobody should invent a complete translation to make the stones chattier.

An even earlier carved sample from San José Mogote is conventionally read “1 Earthquake.” Much later, Juan de Córdova’s 1578 grammar printed the Latin-script Zapotec word “Niça,” meaning “water.” These samples belong to different centuries and writing systems. Together they show a long history of writing, while modern Zapotec varieties must not be treated as one unchanged ancient language.

The city collected goods such as maize, beans and squash from communities it controlled, hosted exchange and made distinctive pottery. As the urban population grew, more specialists produced everyday wares for other households rather than every family making every pot. A chipped cooking bowl may look humble in a museum, but it can reveal an economy of farmers, carriers, potters and market exchange.

The official guide identifies a female ruler on the great VG-2 stone and a male ruler called 13 Owl on another monument. That does not prove equal power for women and men, but it warns against drawing an all-male government simply because later histories remembered more men. Stone monuments are political selections, not a complete census of leadership.

sections.title: Homes, food, children and a serious ball game

items.text: Burials often lay inside household compounds: in masonry tombs, stone-lined cists, bedrock pits or even storage pits, ovens and rubbish spaces reused for the dead. Formal tombs held important members of a family, and painted processions may portray ancestors. Home, cooking, storage, family memory and death could occupy the same domestic world instead of separate modern-style zones.

Maize supplied much of the food, with beans and squash also central. Because the summit was not prime farmland, rural households and city residents depended on one another. Families diverted small amounts of rainwater, tended fields and useful dry-land plants, carried produce uphill and traded for pottery. Dinner rested on a supply chain with far more climbing than a modern grocery run.

Children appear in archaeology even though they left no diaries. A study of two middle- or high-status household compounds found younger children buried in patios and older children more often beneath room floors, with offerings differing by age and status. That evidence concerns death and family ritual, not every child’s daily routine, and two households cannot stand for a whole city.

Monte Albán had five ball courts. INAH describes the game as part of ordinary and ceremonial life and as one way communities could address disputes involving land, tribute or trade. The best-preserved court is sunken and double-T-shaped. It was closer to ritual sport, theatre and negotiation combined than to recess: losing probably did not earn a juice box.

sections.title: Learning, medicine, rainwater and the toilet question

items.text: No surviving sign says “Monte Albán Elementary School.” Yet scribes learned a demanding glyph system, calendar specialists tracked dates, potters repeated complex techniques and builders laid out drains and monuments. Archaeology shows trained knowledge, but not whether children learned in formal classrooms, household workshops, temples or several settings. Honest education history sometimes begins with what the evidence cannot tell us.

Bones in the site museum show trepanation, intentional head shaping, altered teeth and stone dental inlays. Trepanation means an opening was made in the skull, but the bone alone does not hand us the patient’s diagnosis, pain relief or surgeon’s instructions. Some procedures may have mixed healing, identity and ritual. Ancient medicine deserves curiosity without pretending every hole has a known story.

Engineers captured and redirected rain around the Main Plaza and ball court, helping supply water and prevent floods. Archaeologists have traced covered drains between public spaces. These channels were excellent storm-water engineering, but they are not proof of a citywide sewer or flush toilets. So the honest toilet answer is frustrating: people certainly relieved themselves, yet no labelled latrine manual survives.

A rainwater network would have demanded planning and upkeep, while a mountaintop city depended on links with farmers below. The evidence does not name whoever cleared each drain or carried each basket. Kid translation: gravity helped water run downhill, which is exactly why supplying people who lived uphill was the harder trick. The marvel was organized work, not a magical endless tap.

sections.title: A famous discovery, a political ending and living Zapotec peoples

items.text: In 1932 Alfonso Caso uncovered the spectacular contents of Tomb 7. Gold, silver, turquoise, crystal, shell and other objects reveal extraordinary craft and far-reaching exchange. Here is the twist: INAH dates this Mixtec collection to 1250-1521, centuries after Monte Albán stopped being a capital. Archaeological location and cultural date are not the same label.

Around 800 to 850 CE, Monte Albán lost its role as the valley’s ruling capital and much of its population dispersed. Researchers describe political fragmentation and large-scale abandonment, but UNESCO says the cause is not established. It was not a movie-style vanishing: people reorganized in other communities, and visitors continued leaving offerings among the old monuments.

Zapotec peoples did not end when one capital declined. Mexico’s language institute recognizes a Zapotec grouping with 62 varieties spoken across historic regions in Oaxaca and southern Veracruz, and communities are deciding how different writing traditions should be standardized. Modern speakers are not museum exhibits or identical descendants of one ancient household; they are living peoples with their own present histories.

ending.text: Monte Albán’s state and capital role ended gradually around 800 to 850 CE as population and power shifted to other centres. The site was never simply erased: later visitors treated it as sacred, Mixtec elites reused tombs, archaeologists and local institutions preserve it, and Zapotec peoples and languages continue. The atlas’s 800 cutoff approximates political change; it is not a date when everyone left or a culture disappeared.
